options.misconception: Using a value length instead of key count
Assuming only one property is enumerable

questions.explanation: for...in visits the enumerable keys a and b, so the concatenated string has length two. The numeric values, including 3493, are never visited by this loop. The printed value is 2, while the alternatives come from assuming only one property is enumerable, counting the letter a twice and using a value length instead of key count.
questions.hint: for...in enumerates property names.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving async — microtasks.

options.misconception: Running the callback before synchronous code

questions.explanation: Synchronous logs run first, then the promise callback drains in the microtask queue, producing start end 3494. Microtasks wait until the current stack is empty. The printed value is start end 3494, while the alternatives come from running the callback before synchronous code, reversing the synchronous logs and treating the promise as immediate.
questions.hint: Promise callbacks are microtasks, not synchronous calls.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving async — timers.

options.misconception: Treating a zero delay as immediate

questions.explanation: setTimeout schedules its callback as a macrotask, so both synchronous logs finish before 3495 appears. A delay of zero does not mean run right now. The printed value is 1 3 3495, while the alternatives come from treating a zero delay as immediate, reversing the synchronous statements and placing the timer callback first.
questions.hint: Timers run after the current synchronous stack clears.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving errors — try catch finally.

options.misconception: Believing finally is skipped after a throw
Swapping the catch and finally order

questions.explanation: The throw enters catch, which logs 'caught', and finally always runs afterwards with 'done'. The finally block executes whether or not an error was thrown. The printed value is caught done, while the alternatives come from swapping the catch and finally order, believing finally is skipped after a throw and believing catch is skipped.
questions.hint: finally runs after catch, even on the error path.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving data — json.

stimulus.body: A program is processing the value 3497.

questions.explanation: JSON.parse turns the text into an object whose n property holds 3497. JSON keys must be quoted, but the parsed value is a regular number. The printed value is 3497, while the alternatives come from assuming parsing loses numeric fields, adding one after parsing and applies a different mistaken operation.
questions.hint: parse converts JSON text into a JavaScript object.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — numeric sort.
questions.explanation: The comparator subtracts to sort numerically ascending, placing the smallest value 2 first. Without a comparator, sort would compare the numbers as strings. Carrying the operation through gives 2; common slips include assuming sort leaves the original order and picking the middle value.
questions.hint: A comparator returning a minus b sorts numbers ascending.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — index of.

options.misconception: Assuming the value is not found

questions.explanation: indexOf returns the zero-based position of the first match; 3499 sits at index zero here. A missing value would yield negative one instead. The printed value is 0, while the alternatives come from using one-based indexing, assuming the value is not found and reporting the array length.
questions.hint: JavaScript array positions begin at zero.
